characters: Akua: a cheerful girl of seven with short natural hair, a yellow school uniform and a satchel with a blue pencil case.
Sefakor: a new girl of seven with braids and a green school uniform, who speaks Ewe at home.
Alhassan: a thoughtful boy of eight in a white school shirt who speaks Hausa at home.
Madam Serwaa: their kind teacher, in a turquoise wax-print dress and round glasses.

narrationPlan.voice: Friendly, bright voice that pronounces each language’s words carefully
narrationPlan.pace: Steady and warm (about 100 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Light xylophone and shaker, with warm layered voices (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Verified thank-you words: Medaase (Twi), Akpé (Ewe), Nagode (Hausa).
Ghanaian classrooms often include children with several home languages; the story invites children to value all of them.

teacherGuide.overview: A story that treats home languages as a classroom strength. The activity after it builds a thank-you wall in the languages your learners know.
learningGoals: Say thank you in at least three languages.
Value the different languages learners speak.
beforeReading: Ask: how do you say thank you at home?
whileReading: Pause at pages 2, 3 and 4 and say each word aloud together.
afterReading: Build a thank-you wall on a door or noticeboard, with each word in the language and in English.
discussion: How did the children show respect for each other’s languages?
Why did the class make the wall?
reflection: Which word on the wall surprised you the most?

support: Let children draw a thank-you picture and dictate the word.
stretch: Teach a family member a new thank-you word and report back.

culturalNotes: Verified thank-you words: Medaase (Twi), Akpé (Ewe), Nagode (Hausa).
Ghanaian classrooms often include children with several home languages; the story invites children to value all of them.
localiseThis: Add the languages actually spoken in your class, including Ga (Oyiwaladɔŋ), Dagbani (M paɣiya), Fante (Medaase) and others.

pronunciation.guidance: Ghanaians often say "uh-KRAH" (stress on the second syllable).
